items.caption:
The best conversations start with a pause.

The small quiet after a question, while the other person decides how much to tell you. Don’t rush to fill it, and the real answer usually comes.

When did a pause change a conversation for you?

Dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres. Inglés: Tell me who you spend time with, and I’ll tell you who you are.

It’s the Spanish cousin of “birds of a feather”. In Spain it’s usually a warning about the company you keep, but friends use it to tease each other too.

Try it with a smile this week, when a friend starts sounding just like their flatmate: “Dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres.”

items.caption:
¿Primera cena en casa de los padres de tu pareja? Inglés: First dinner at your partner’s parents’ house?

Here’s what to do and what to say, from hello to goodbye. Save it for the night before.

Al llegar: Gracias por invitarme. Tenéis una casa preciosa.
Inglés: Thanks for having me. You have a lovely home.

En la mesa: Esto está buenísimo. ¿Quién te enseñó a hacer este plato?
Inglés: This is delicious. Who taught you to make this dish?

Con el café: ¿Y vosotros cómo os conocisteis?
Inglés: And how did you two meet?

Al despedirte: Muchas gracias por todo. Me he sentido como en casa.
Inglés: Thank you for everything. I felt right at home.

Not sure whether to use tú or usted? Start with usted. They’ll soon tell you «puedes tutearme», which means you can call them tú. The formal versions are on the slides.

What did they ask you at your first dinner? Tell us below ↓

For more questions for your partner’s family, read “Talking with your partner’s family in another language: questions that help” in our Journal. The link is in today’s story.

items.caption:
Hoy recordamos contando historias. Inglés: Today, we remember by telling stories.

In Spain, 1 November is el Día de Todos los Santos, All Saints’ Day. Families take flowers to the cemetery, and bakeries fill with huesos de santo (little marzipan “saints’ bones”) and buñuelos de viento (light, airy fritters).

In Mexico, el Día de Muertos runs from 1 to 2 November. Families build an ofrenda, an altar with photos, marigolds and the favourite food of the people they miss, and tell their stories out loud.

Whose story would you tell today? Share it below, or tell someone at home.

#diademuertos #todoslossantos #spanishculture #learnspanish #dimemas

items.caption:
La vecina de enfrente te saluda cada mañana. Inglés: The neighbour across the street says hello every morning.

«Buenos días». «Buenos días». Y cada uno a lo suyo. Mañana, prueba con una pregunta más:
¿Cuánto tiempo llevas viviendo en el barrio?
Inglés: How long have you lived round here?
Formal: ¿Cuánto tiempo lleva viviendo en el barrio?

Neighbours who’ve been on the street for years know it better than any guide. Once they’ve told you, ask where they’d send you. It takes two minutes at the door.

From our Journal: “They liked you more than you think”, on why we leave a chat sure it went worse than it did. The link is in today’s story.

#movingtospain #learnspanish #spanishconversation #dimemas

Tercer intercambio y se os han acabado los temas. Inglés: Your third exchange, and you’ve run out of things to talk about.

Ya habéis hablado del tiempo. Dos veces. Prueba con esta:
¿Qué sabe todo el mundo en tu país que aquí nadie entiende?
Inglés: What does everyone know back home that nobody gets here?

It works in both languages, which is the point of an exchange. One of you asks, the other tells. Then swap.

From our Journal: “How to run a language exchange that doesn’t fizzle out”. The link is in today’s story.

Diciembre: el mes de las mesas largas. Inglés: December: the month of long tables.

There is a particular feeling to sitting down for a meal you did not grow up with. Someone passes you something and says a word you half-recognise. You eat what you are given and try to follow the conversation.

In Spain, December is structured around meals in a way that feels almost liturgical. The table is where the month happens: Nochebuena, the post-lottery lunch, the Sunday after Christmas when the whole family comes back again. Sobremesa, the time you sit after the food is gone, can stretch for hours. Nobody is in a hurry to leave.

If you are spending December inside someone else's traditions for the first time, there is a Journal piece waiting for you. It is about the conversations that make a new place feel like home. Link in bio.

A veces no te sale la palabra. Inglés: Sometimes you don't have the word.

Turn the sound up.

There is a particular moment, mid-sentence, mid-thought, when you reach for a word in another language and come back empty. You gesture. You pause. You find a way around it.

Researchers who study second language acquisition call this a communication strategy: the workaround is not failure, it is fluency in progress. But in the moment, it can feel like standing in a corridor with the door shut.

Spanish has a word, añoranza, that sits somewhere between longing and nostalgia. English has neither quite caught up with it nor quite needed to. Sometimes the gap between languages is not a problem to solve. It is a window into how another culture has learned to see.

If you have ever felt the gap, the Monday letter is for you. One email a week on language and connection. Sign up at the link in bio.

¿Qué preguntas haces cuando alguien llega a tu mesa? Inglés: What questions do you ask when someone comes to your table?

The first question most people reach for is: where are you from? It is not a bad question. It is just the least interesting one available.

Asked too soon, 'where are you from' can work less as curiosity and more as a way of placing someone before you have decided how to treat them. It can feel like categorisation dressed up as conversation.

There are better questions. Not clever questions, just ones that leave room for a real answer. What did you eat for breakfast when you were a child? What is a place you think about more than you expected to? What is something you have learned to do here that you could not do before?

There is more on this in our Journal: “The question that turned dinner into a conversation”. The link is in today’s story.

El lugar llega después de la conversación. Inglés: The place comes after the conversation.

There is a moment, in a new city, when you stop translating and start listening. Not to words exactly, but to rhythm, to tone, to the particular noise a neighbourhood makes on a Monday evening.

Researchers who study what is called place attachment find that belonging rarely arrives through a landmark or an address. It tends to arrive through a repeated exchange: the woman who runs the bread stall learning how you take your coffee, the porter who asks after your mother. Language is the hinge.

items.caption:
El puente más esperado del año termina hoy. Inglés: The most anticipated long weekend of the year ends today.

In Spain, when a bank holiday falls on a Tuesday or a Thursday, the Monday or Friday in between is called a puente: a bridge. The country crosses it together. Shops close. Motorways fill. Families sit down to lunch at two in the afternoon and are still there at six.

The Feast of the Inmaculada Concepción on 8 December is one of the most reliable puentes in the calendar, especially when it combines with Día de la Constitución on the 6th. The four-day stretch that results has its own texture: slower speech, longer meals, the kind of afternoon where someone always says 'una más': just one more.

For anyone navigating a new language, a puente is unexpectedly useful. The pace drops. People have time to listen. The pressure of a busy Tuesday morning disappears.

What do you do with the extra time?

El castellano es la lengua oficial del Estado. Inglés: Castilian is the official language of the state.

But that is not the whole sentence. Article 3 of Spain's 1978 constitution continues: the other Spanish languages shall also be official in their respective autonomous communities, in line with their statutes. Today that includes Catalan, Basque, Galician and Valencian.

It was, and remains, a rare thing: a constitution that names language explicitly and acknowledges that a country and its languages are not always the same shape.

For anyone moving to certain parts of Spain, this is not an abstract point. In Barcelona a shopkeeper may greet you in Catalan. In San Sebastián a street sign might be in Basque first. The constitution made room for that.

Language is never just grammar. It is always also history.

items.caption:
¿En qué idioma piensas cuando importa? Inglés: Which language do you think in when it matters?

Researchers working with bilingual families have found something consistent: when the stakes go up, the first language often comes back. People who have spoken a second language fluently for years will switch, sometimes mid-sentence, when they are frightened, or in love, or trying to say something true.

It is not a failure of fluency. Linguists describe it as emotional salience: certain feelings are simply stored where language was first learned.

This has a practical side, too. If you are the person across the table who does not share that first language, there is a moment you will recognise: the other person is looking for a word that does not exist in the language you share. What you do in that moment matters more than you think.

We wrote about this in the Journal. Link in bio.

If you would like the Monday letter, the sign-up is there too.

#languagelearning #learnspanish #bilinguallife #movingtospain #profluency

Un idioma no es un nivel. Inglés: A language is not a level.

There is a habit, in language learning, of measuring everything. A2. B1. C2. The level becomes the identity. But studies in bilingual households consistently show that emotional register does not follow the exam table.

A grandmother who has lived in London for forty years and speaks excellent English will often, when upset or tender or very funny, reach for Spanish. Not because her English is insufficient. Because the feeling lives in Spanish.

The reverse is equally true. A British person who has lived in Madrid for a decade may find that the language they count in, or curse in, or use when they cannot sleep, is still English. The second language carries the daily life. The first carries the interior one.

This is worth knowing if you are the person sitting opposite. A confident speaker going quiet is not losing their language. They may be looking for the version that fits.

There is a Dime Más card that fits: “¿Qué emoción crees que deberías expresar más en el futuro?” What emotion do you think you should express more in the future? It tends to open things.

What language do your quietest thoughts arrive in?

#learnspanish #bilinguallife #languagelearning #movingtospain #profluency

In Spanish there is a verb, convivir, that goes further than 'to coexist'. It means something closer to sharing a life, not just a room. La primera cena is the beginning of that.

items.caption:
Sobremesa: el tiempo que queda después de comer. Inglés: Sobremesa: the time that remains after the meal.

In Spain, leaving the table the moment the food is gone is, quietly and without anyone saying so, considered a little rude. The meal is not just the eating. The conversation after is part of it. La sobremesa can last an hour. It can last three.

There is no direct English word for it. 'Lingering' points in the right direction but feels apologetic. Spanish simply named the thing, which suggests the culture decided it mattered enough to keep.

Sociologists who study commensality (the rituals around shared eating) note that the transition moment, when plates are cleared but nobody moves, is when the most significant personal conversation tends to happen. The meal loosens things.

When did you last let a meal run that long?

items.caption:
El primer hola que importó. Inglés: The first hello that mattered.

Today is International Migrants Day. Across the world, people are living in a language that was not the one they grew up in. Some have been doing it for a year. Some for thirty.

Researchers who study migration and belonging have noted something that comes up again and again: people rarely name arrival as the moment a new country began to feel like home. They name a conversation. Not a form filled in, not a bureaucratic hurdle cleared, but an exchange that went beyond logistics: someone who asked a real question and stayed for the answer.

In Spanish the verb estrenar means to use something for the first time, to break it in. Making a place your own begins, so often, with a single exchange.

If you have moved somewhere and found your footing in a new language, what was the conversation that shifted something?

The Journal article on this is in the link in our bio.

#internationalmigrantsday #movingabroad #learningspanish #bilinguallife #languageandbelonging

El idioma del consuelo no siempre es el primero que aprendiste. Inglés: The language of comfort is not always the first one you learned.

Researchers studying bilingual experience have consistently found that strong emotions tend to feel more immediate in the language a person grew up speaking. Grief in a second language can feel slightly muffled. Anger in a first language can arrive faster than you expect.

But it is not always that simple. Some bilingual people report that their second language gives them a useful distance: it is easier to discuss something painful in the language that carries less emotional charge. The very thing that makes a second language feel thinner can, sometimes, make it easier to enter a difficult room.

In Spanish the word ternura (tenderness, warmth towards someone you care for) is used more easily in everyday speech than its English equivalent. Whether that reflects the language or the culture around it is a question worth sitting with.

Which language do you reach for when something is hard?

The Journal article on this is in the link in our bio.

La noche más larga del año. Inglés: The longest night of the year.

The winter solstice falls quietly, without a ceremony in most places. In Spain it is called el solsticio de invierno, and for a culture that has always kept late hours, one more dark evening barely registers. But there is something worth sitting with before the noise of the festive week arrives.

In Spanish the word for nightfall is el anochecer, a noun made from the verb anochecer, to grow dark. It happens to you. You do not make it dark; the dark comes. There is something honest about a language that treats the end of daylight as something that arrives rather than something you lose.

Tonight is a good one for a slow conversation. No agenda, no plan.

What do you do with a long evening when you let yourself have one?

items.caption:
Toque o no toque, hoy lo vivimos juntos. Inglés: Today we win, or we don't, but we do it together.

The Lotería de Navidad draw began in 1812, making it one of the oldest lotteries in the world. The format has barely changed. Children from the Colegio de San Ildefonso in Madrid sing out the numbers, and their voices are broadcast across the country every 22 December.

What makes it Spanish is not the prize but the structure. A décimo costs twenty euros, so lots of people share one, buying a participación (a small share of a ticket) from their bar, their office or a local club. Neighbours who barely speak all year find themselves watching the same screen on the same morning.

There is a word for the feeling when your number does not come up: quedarse sin premio. Literally, to be left without a prize. But you still had the morning together. The shared ticket was never really about the money.

Who do you share things with, even when there is nothing to win?

#loteriadenavidad #elgordo #spanishculture #learnspanish #navidad

Mañana empieza esta noche. Inglés: Tomorrow begins tonight.

In Spain, Nochebuena on 24 December is the main event, not Christmas Day. The meal is almost always at home, almost always with family, and the preparation begins well before the day itself.

The kitchen the night before has its own particular atmosphere: stock on a low heat, the radio on in the background, someone peeling something at the table. It is the Spanish version of a dress rehearsal, except nobody calls it that.

The word for this kind of quiet domestic industry is trajín, a busyness that is purposeful rather than rushed. You do not eliminate the trajín; you move through it together.

What does your night before look like?

Feliz Navidad dice más que su traducción. Inglés: Feliz Navidad means more than it translates.

There are phrases that carry weight not because of what they mean word by word but because of when you say them. Feliz Navidad is one. Buenas noches on a night like this is another. They are not translations of a feeling; they are the feeling.

Research in bilingualism suggests that second-language speakers often find emotional language harder to access under pressure, but easier to receive. Hearing a phrase in someone's language, even imperfectly, tends to land differently than hearing your own.

Tonight, whatever table you are at, one phrase in someone else's language goes a long way.

#feliznavidad #christmas #learnspanish #spanishculture #bilinguallife

El día después. Inglés: The day after.

In Britain, 26 December is Boxing Day. These days it means cold cuts, a long walk, a film on the sofa, possibly a queue outside a shop.

In Spain, 26 December is San Esteban (Sant Esteve in Catalan) in some regions, a public holiday in Catalonia and others, but for many it is simply a working day. The leftovers are yesterday's news and the office is open.

What both cultures share is the strange particular atmosphere of the day after the big meal. The table has been cleared. The effort of the night before is over. Something slightly looser takes its place.

In Spanish, leftovers are las sobras, from the verb sobrar, to be surplus to requirements. There is no shame in las sobras. You eat them standing at the fridge at noon and call it lunch.

If your table still has people around it, Dime Más is good for the day after.

What does your 26 December look like?

items.caption:
Hoy no te creas todo lo que lees. Inglés: Today, don't believe everything you read.

Spain's 28 December is los Inocentes, the country's own April Fools' Day, named after the feast of the Holy Innocents. The newspapers print a fake story. The radio runs a spoof interview. At the bar, someone will stick a paper monigote on your back without you noticing. Children shout inocenteeee when the joke lands.

Humour is one of the last things to arrive in a second language and one of the first things people miss. Timing, register, the exact weight of a word: none of it translates cleanly. You can know every verb and still not be sure whether a joke has landed or caused offence.

That gap is real. And closing it, even a little, is one of the better feelings language gives you.

items.caption:
Doce uvas. Doce segundos. Una promesa. Inglés: Twelve grapes. Twelve seconds. A promise.

On the stroke of midnight on 31 December, Spain stops. Everywhere, in living rooms, in squares, in bars with the television turned up, people eat one grape for each bell of the Puerta del Sol clock. Twelve grapes, twelve months ahead, one shared minute across the whole country.

The tradition is thought to date from around 1909, when wine growers in Alicante had a glut of late-harvest grapes and the custom caught on. Now it is simply what you do. The Spanish call it las uvas de la suerte, the grapes of luck, though it feels less like luck and more like a collective breath before the year turns.

What strikes most people who do it for the first time in Spain is how quiet the room goes. Twelve seconds is not long, but it is long enough to feel.

Feliz Nochevieja. See you on the other side.

items.caption:
We're looking for about 40 people in the UK to test Pocket It, our new iPhone app.

Pocket It helps you find the right words for real conversations in another language and keeps them close for when you need them. It covers Spanish, French, Portuguese, Japanese, Korean, German and Italian. In the clip, a Spanish line from the Meet with laughter deck plays in a native voice and goes into Pocket. Then Sense shows how to say "many thanks".

It's an early test build, and we'd like to hear wherever something feels wrong. Trying it takes about ten minutes. It's free on iPhone through Apple's TestFlight app. Testing runs until Friday 4 December.

Sign up at profluency.co.uk/ranges/pocket-it/ and we'll email you the invitation straight away. The link is in our bio too.

items.caption:
How would you tell a friend that you've done something daft, in their language?

Antes he hecho una tontería. ¿Quieres la versión corta?
Inglés: I did something ridiculous earlier. Want the short version?

Spanish is one of seven languages in Pocket It, our new iPhone app, and this line comes from its Meet with laughter deck. Play it as often as you like, then tap to keep it in Pocket for the next time something daft happens.

We're still looking for testers in the UK until Friday 4 December. The test build costs nothing and runs on iPhone through Apple's TestFlight app. Sign up at profluency.co.uk/ranges/pocket-it/ (it's in our bio) and the invitation comes straight to your inbox.
